questions.q: In standard HTTPS, which side proves its identity via a certificate?
options: Only the server presents a certificate; the client's identity is handled separately by an Authentication Profile
Only the client presents a certificate
Neither side presents a certificate
Both sides present certificates, by default, on every HTTPS connection
questions.explain: Standard HTTPS is one-directional trust: the server proves itself to the client. The client's own identity is proven separately — e.g. via Basic Auth or OAuth.

questions.q: What does mutual TLS (mutual authentication) add on top of standard HTTPS?
options: It removes the need for any Authentication Profile at all
It replaces OAuth access tokens with API keys
Both the client and the server present and verify certificates — the handshake fails if either side's certificate doesn't check out
It only applies to SOAP-based integrations, not REST
questions.explain: Mutual TLS requires both sides to prove their identity with certificates, not just the server, and the connection fails before any request runs if either certificate is invalid.

questions.q: What kind of integration does this lesson describe as the real use case for mutual TLS?
options: Any integration that needs to move faster to set up than Basic Auth
Highly sensitive integrations, such as financial or government systems, that require certificate-based identity verification on both ends
Integrations where the external API has no token endpoint at all
Integrations that only ever run inside a sandbox instance
questions.explain: Mutual TLS is real overhead — both sides need certificates and a renewal process — so it's reserved for cases where certificate-based verification on both ends is a hard requirement.

questions.q: How is an API key typically sent to an external API?
options: As a base64-encoded username and password
As a client certificate presented during the TLS handshake
It cannot be sent over HTTP headers at all
As a shared secret string in a custom HTTP header, such as X-API-Key
questions.explain: An API key is a plain shared-secret string passed in a custom header the external API recognizes — configured on the REST Message's HTTP Headers, not an OAuth profile.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe API keys as generally less secure than OAuth access tokens?
options: Most API key implementations have no built-in expiration and no scope model, so a leaked key is often all-or-nothing access until someone manually rotates it
API keys are always sent unencrypted, even over HTTPS
API keys cannot be used with REST Messages in ServiceNow
OAuth tokens are encrypted and API keys are not, even over the same HTTPS connection
questions.explain: Unlike OAuth tokens, which expire and can be scoped, API keys are typically static, all-or-nothing credentials — the same practical weakness Basic Auth has.
